Paper_name: More or less of me and you: self-relevance augments the effects of item probability on stimulus prioritization
Summary: In three shape-label matching experiments (Sui et al. 2012 style), the study examined how the frequency of self- versus friend-related shapes interacts with self-relevance in stimulus prioritization. Participants learned shape-label associations (self, friend) and then judged whether shape-label pairs matched, while prior expectancies about stimulus frequency were provided. With equal frequencies (Exp 1), a standard self-prioritization effect emerged. In confirmatory (Exp 2) and dis-confirmatory (Exp 3) contexts, frequently presented stimuli were prioritized, an effect most pronounced for self-relevant items. Hierarchical drift diffusion modeling traced the effects to the rate of information uptake, which was faster for self-related stimuli.
Author: Saga L. Svensson, Marius Golubickis, Hollie Maclean, Johanna K. Falbén, Linn M. Persson, Dimitra Tsamadi, Siobhan Caughey, Arash Sahraie, C. Neil Macrae
Conclusion: Stimulus frequency and personal relevance jointly shape stimulus prioritization in shape-label matching. When self- and friend-related shapes appeared equally often (Exp 1), a self-prioritization effect emerged on matching trials. In both confirmatory (Exp 2) and dis-confirmatory (Exp 3) task contexts, frequently encountered stimuli were prioritized, with the effect most pronounced for self-relevant items. HDDM analyses indicated the effects were driven by the rate of information uptake (faster for self-related stimuli), with expectancy disconfirmation influencing friend- but not self-related processing, suggesting self-related beliefs are relatively resistant to updating.
